body.statement: Under effective \(K\)-valued inputs, \(\operatorname{Cert}_{uv,m,G}(B,Q)\) terminates and is sound and complete. It returns incompatibility exactly when \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\); conditional on \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\ne\varnothing\), it returns one rational function exactly when \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) consists of one rational function; otherwise it returns two attained stable pairs \((A,D),(A',D')\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) satisfying \((A_{vu}-A'_{vu})^2+(A_{vu}A'_{vv}-A'_{vu}A_{vv})^2>0\). The certificate remains complete for zero diagonals, zero queried edges, open fibers, positive-dimensional fibers, and branch mergers.
body.justification: A total formula-or-ambiguity output replaces numerical root selection by an auditable causal identification certificate.
body.gap: Classical CAD decides semialgebraic formulas and classical root methods select branches; neither provides this target-aware graph-recursive contract with covariance filtering and exact transfer-distinct witnesses.
body.consumer: Software for subsampled process-DAG analysis can refuse false singleton answers and furnish two explicit observationally equivalent causal explanations when identification fails.
body.proof_tex:
Fix the effective \(K\)-valued matrices \(B,Q\), the supplied graph \(G\), and the known integer \(m\geq 2\).  For each compatible structural pair \((A,D)\), the causal target is the transfer \(h_{uv}(z)=A_{vu}z/(1-A_{vv}z)\).  By contrast, \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is the image of the compatible structural fiber under this transfer map.  Thus the observed coarse law identifies the causal target precisely when this image is a singleton; this relationship will be proved by the certificate rather than imposed as a definition of the causal target.

Put
\[
 \mathcal I_G
 =\{(i,i):i\in V\}\cup
   \{(i,j):j<i\text{ and }j\to i\text{ in }G\}.
\]
For every \((i,j)\in\mathcal I_G\), introduce a real variable \(a_{ij}\), and introduce real variables \(d_1,\ldots,d_d\).  Let \(\widetilde A(a)\) have entry \(a_{ij}\) on \(\mathcal I_G\) and zero elsewhere, and let \(\widetilde D(d)=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_d)\).  The lower-triangular and graph-support restrictions in the definition of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) are therefore imposed by this coordinate parametrization.

Consider the finite system
\[
 \bigl[\widetilde A(a)^m\bigr]_{ij}=B_{ij}
 \quad(i,j\in V),                                                   \tag{1}
\]
\[
 \left[\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\widetilde A(a)^r\widetilde D(d)
                    \bigl(\widetilde A(a)^r\bigr)^\top\right]_{ij}
 =Q_{ij}
 \quad(i,j\in V),                                                   \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 -1<a_{ii}<1\quad(i\in V),
 \qquad d_i>0\quad(i\in V).                                        \tag{3}
\]
Every left-hand side in (1)--(2) is a polynomial in finitely many variables with coefficients in \(K\), by the effective-input assumption.  Since \(\widetilde A(a)\) is triangular,
\[
 \det\!\left(\lambda I-\widetilde A(a)\right)
   =\prod_{i=1}^d(\lambda-a_{ii}),
 \qquad
 \rho\!\left(\widetilde A(a)\right)=\max_i|a_{ii}|.
\]
Consequently the first collection of strict inequalities in (3) is equivalent to stability.  Moreover, for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb R^d\),
\[
 x^\top\widetilde D(d)x=\sum_{i=1}^d d_i x_i^2>0
\]
if and only if every \(d_i>0\).  Hence the second collection in (3) is equivalent to \(\widetilde D(d)\succ0\).  It follows from the definition of the compatible fiber that
\[
 (a,d)\longmapsto\bigl(\widetilde A(a),\widetilde D(d)\bigr)         \tag{4}
\]
is a bijection from the realization of (1)--(3) onto \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  In particular, this encoding neither adds boundary points nor replaces strict positivity or strict stability by their closures.

For a triangular matrix, the diagonal part of (1) is
\[
 a_{ii}^{m}=B_{ii},\qquad i\in V.                                  \tag{5}
\]
Because \(K\) is an effective real closed field, its effective arithmetic, order tests, and real-root isolation enumerate the real roots of each equation (5) and decide the stability inequalities in (3).  There is exactly one real root of \(x^m=b\) when \(m\) is odd.  When \(m\) is even, there are no real roots for \(b<0\), one for \(b=0\), and two for \(b>0\).  Thus there are finitely many surviving diagonal branches, and their coordinates are represented exactly in \(K\).  If no branch survives, (4) shows that the compatible fiber is empty.

Fix one surviving branch and process off-diagonal pairs \((v,u)\) in increasing order of \(v-u\), as prescribed by the graph-recursive root map.  The path-expansion lemma gives
\[
 a_{vu}C_m(a_{vv},a_{uu})
   =B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}(\widetilde A(a)).                               \tag{6}
\]
Every off-diagonal coordinate occurring on the right side of (6) has smaller endpoint gap.  The diagonal entries in
\[
 c_{vu}:=C_m(a_{vv},a_{uu})                                        \tag{7}
\]
are fixed on the branch, so \(c_{vu}\in K\).  The divided-difference zero-set lemma, together with the exact sign tests in \(K\), decides whether \(c_{vu}=0\).  In particular, the odd-factor case \(a_{vv}=a_{uu}=0\) and the even-factor case \(a_{vv}=-a_{uu}\) are retained as singular cases rather than divided through.

If \(u\to v\) is graph-allowed and \(c_{vu}\neq0\), equation (6) is equivalent to the unique substitution
\[
 a_{vu}
 =\frac{B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}(\widetilde A(a))}{c_{vu}}.                 \tag{8}
\]
This division is made only after the nonzero test.  Since \(c_{vu}^{-1}\in K\) is fixed on the branch, substituting (8) into later transition equations and into the covariance equations produces polynomials over \(K\) in the residual variables; there is no variable denominator.  If \(c_{vu}=0\), the coordinate is not eliminated and the induced equation
\[
 B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}(\widetilde A(a))=0                                \tag{9}
\]
is retained.  If the edge is forbidden, \(a_{vu}=0\) by the support parametrization and the transition equation (9) is again retained, irrespective of the value of \(c_{vu}\).

Induction over the endpoint gap proves exactness of the recursion.  At a nonsingular allowed coordinate, every solution of the pre-substitution system must have the value (8), while every solution of the substituted system lifts uniquely through (8).  At a singular or forbidden coordinate, no residual variable or compatibility equation is discarded.  The induction is applicable because the path-expansion lemma places only smaller-gap off-diagonal coordinates in the remainder.  After the finitely many pairs have been processed, every transition equation not already used for an exact substitution, every covariance equation in (2), and every strict inequality in (3) remains imposed after the accumulated substitutions.  Therefore, if \(\mathfrak R_b\) denotes the residual semialgebraic realization on diagonal branch \(b\) and \(\operatorname{Rec}_b\) denotes reconstruction by the substitutions, then
\[
 \mathcal S(B,Q;G)
   =\bigcup_b \operatorname{Rec}_b(\mathfrak R_b).                 \tag{10}
\]
This is literal set equality, not equality after topological or algebraic closure.

Each \(\mathfrak R_b\) is a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict polynomial inequalities over \(K\).  There are finitely many branches and finitely many variables.  The effective CAD decision-and-sampling lemma therefore implies that CAD terminates on every branch, decides whether \(\mathfrak R_b\) is empty, and returns an exact represented sample point whenever it is nonempty.  By (10), all branch systems are empty if and only if \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\).  This proves termination, soundness, and completeness of the incompatibility output.

It remains to classify the transfer fiber.  Suppose that the compatible fiber is nonempty, take two compatible points, and write
\[
 p=A_{vu},\quad q=A_{vv},\qquad
 p'=A'_{vu},\quad q'=A'_{vv}.
\]
Stability gives \(|q|<1\) and \(|q'|<1\).  Hence, for every \(z\in\mathbb T\),
\[
 |qz|<1,\qquad |q'z|<1,
\]
so neither \(1-qz\) nor \(1-q'z\) vanishes.  Since also \(z\neq0\) on \(\mathbb T\), cross multiplication and cancellation of \(z\) are valid.  The two transfers agree on \(\mathbb T\) if and only if
\[
 p(1-q'z)=p'(1-qz)\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb T.             \tag{11}
\]
The difference between the sides of (11) is
\[
 (p-p')+(p'q-pq')z.                                                 \tag{12}
\]
Evaluating (12) at \(z=1\) and \(z=-1\) shows that it vanishes on \(\mathbb T\) if and only if both coefficients vanish.  Thus
\[
 h_{p,q}=h_{p',q'}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p=p'\ \text{ and }\ pq'=p'q,                                    \tag{13}
\]
and, since all four coefficients are real,
\[
 h_{p,q}\neq h_{p',q'}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Delta(p,q,p',q')
 :=(p-p')^2+(pq'-p'q)^2>0.                                        \tag{14}
\]
Equation (13) correctly treats all pairs \((0,q)\) as representing the same zero transfer; equality of coefficient pairs is neither required nor used.

For every ordered pair of diagonal branches, take two copies of their complete residual systems and append the strict polynomial inequality (14), expressed after reconstruction.  The resulting finite union of two-copy systems is feasible if and only if two points of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) have unequal transfers, by (10) and (14).  The CAD lemma decides this feasibility and, when it holds, supplies exact residual sample points.  Reconstruction yields attained pairs
\[
 (A,D),(A',D')\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)
\]
satisfying
\[
 (A_{vu}-A'_{vu})^2
 +(A_{vu}A'_{vv}-A'_{vu}A_{vv})^2>0.
\]
Their strict stability and innovation-positivity inequalities are inherited from their one-copy branch systems.  This proves soundness of the ambiguity output, while the feasibility equivalence proves its completeness.

If every two-copy system is infeasible, (14) says that every two compatible points yield the same transfer.  An exact sample from any nonempty one-copy branch supplies \((p,q)\) and hence the common exact rational function
\[
 z\longmapsto\frac{pz}{1-qz}.
\]
Conversely, if \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is a singleton, no two-copy system can satisfy (14), and the certificate returns this common function.  Thus the singleton output is equivalent to point identification of the causal transfer, and the three advertised outputs are exhaustive.

The same equivalences cover every stated exceptional case.  Zero diagonal roots remain among the solutions of (5) and enter a residual singular system whenever their divided difference vanishes.  A graph-forbidden queried edge, or an allowed queried edge forced to zero by compatibility, is treated correctly by (13).  The CAD lemma applies directly to open and positive-dimensional fibers with the strict inequalities (3).  Branch duplication or merger cannot change the result because (10) is a union and the two-copy test ranges over every ordered branch pair.  No rank, overlap, conditioning, or limiting condition is invoked, and the sole divisions in the recursion occur under the explicit nonvanishing condition in (8).

For the first required exact stress test, take \(d=2\), \(m=3\), let \(G\) contain \(1\to2\), and set \(B=0\) and \(Q=I_2\).  Define
\[
 A_{\pm}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ \pm\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D_{\pm}=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\tfrac34\right).
\]
Then \(A_{\pm}^2=0\), and hence
\[
 A_{\pm}^3=0=B,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A_{\pm}^rD_{\pm}(A_{\pm}^r)^\top
 =D_{\pm}+A_{\pm}D_{\pm}A_{\pm}^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\tfrac34\right)
  +\operatorname{diag}\!\left(0,\tfrac14\right)
 =I_2.
\]
Both points satisfy the strict inequalities \(\rho(A_{\pm})=0<1\) and \(D_{\pm}\succ0\), while their transfers are \(z/2\) and \(-z/2\).  They are attained, strictly stable, strictly innovation-positive, transfer-distinct witnesses, so the exact two-copy test cannot return either a singleton or a boundary-only artifact.

For the second stress test, let \(d=2\), \(m=2\), and let \((A,D)\) be any compatible point with \(A_{21}\neq0\).  The lower-triangular and graph-support zeros are preserved by \(A\mapsto-A\), as are stability and positivity of \(D\), while
\[
 (-A)^2=A^2,
 \qquad
 D+(-A)D(-A)^\top=D+ADA^\top.
\]
Thus \((-A,D)\) is a second compatible point for the same \((B,Q)\).  With \(p=A_{21}\), \(q=A_{22}\), \(p'=-p\), and \(q'=-q\),
\[
 \Delta(p,q,-p,-q)
 =(2p)^2+\{p(-q)-(-p)q\}^2
 =4p^2>0.
\]
Consequently every nonzero-edge two-variable \(m=2\) compatible case retains its global sign pair, as required.
